items.excerpt: Israel presses ahead with West Bank operation as election approaches TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — The Israeli military is pressing ahead with a massive operation in the occupied West Bank that has displaced hundreds of Palestinians. The move follows a gun attack in Hebron on Friday that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others. As Israel approaches a tense election, the military has placed major restrictions on Palestinian movement. On Sunday, they announced that most Palestinian workers with permits would not be allowed into Israeli settlements for work. The military claims to have operated in over 400 locations over the weekend, arresting 40 Palestinians linked to Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad. Brazil votes in a tense Lula vs Bolsonaro runoff with US influence over Latin America at stake RIO DE JANEIRO (AP) — Brazilians are choosing between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro in a polarizing presidential election. The vote will determine if the U.S. expands its influence in the region. Polls show a close race. Lula is a left-of-center veteran facing Bolsonaro, who is an ally of President Donald Trump and the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flávio Bolsonaro led in the first round. Both candidates have faced corruption allegations. Lula portrays Bolsonaro as a threat to democracy while Bolsonaro promises economic reforms. The election reflects Brazil's divided political landscape with significant implications for U.S.-Brazil relations. More than 400,000 protest across France, challenging Macron as Paris clashes erupt PARIS (AP) — Clashes erupted in Paris as a mass march drew to a close Saturday. More than 400,000 people rallied across France over school funding and soaring living costs, challenging President Emmanuel Macron. Police made nearly 1,000 arrests. The Paris march began peacefully but turned violent near its endpoint. Masked protesters hurled objects and fireworks at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons. The Interior Ministry reported 410,000 protesters nationwide, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000. This unrest is testing Macron's authority in the final months of his presidency before elections in May. Ukraine and Russia eye new peace talks — and Melania Trump's mission — but steep obstacles remain KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine and Russia have signaled willingness to resume peace talks and back a humanitarian mission led by U.S. First lady Melania Trump, but deep disagreements over territory and security guarantees underscore obstacles to ending the war. U.S. President Donald Trump is pushing for a new round of negotiations, potentially in mid-November, as Russia continues to demand control of Ukrainian regions it illegally annexed but does not fully control. Kyiv rejects any suggestion of unilateral withdrawal and says stronger Western pressure on Moscow is needed to advance peace efforts. Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump has cast his ballot in the midterm elections, voting for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally. Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location together Saturday after Trump spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. He has also campaigned for Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon. Saudi Arabia reopens airport as attacks by Houthi rebels persist, and other Mideast news Saudi Arabia has reopened its main airport for international flights after strikes by Yemen's Houthi rebels knocked it out of service. On Sunday, the kingdom intercepted and destroyed a missile and drone fired by the Houthis. Meanwhile, Israel is conducting a military operation in the West Bank following an attack that killed two Israeli soldiers. This comes just days before Israel’s election, seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Netanyahu’s leadership. In other news, Iran’s foreign minister dismissed threats of war, and a Libyan leader rejected comments by U.S. President Donald Trump labeling Libya as "terror-infested." Musk says he was behind Starlink speed restriction after service in Ukraine is restored KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to previous speeds, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He announced Saturday that the restoration began overnight, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian drones. It comes as U.S. envoys have pushed for an end to the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. A localized ceasefire was also brokered Friday by first lady Melania Trump in Ukraine's Kherson region. The limitations on Starshield had alarmed Ukraine's military, adding to tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Meanwhile, missile attacks and power blackouts continue in the region. Soldiers guard center of Milan as thousands of protesters march in cities across Europe MILAN (AP) — Thousands of young people marched through Italian cities like Milan, Rome, and Turin on Saturday. Authorities deployed soldiers in Milan, where previous protests turned violent, but the demonstrations remained peaceful. There were brief clashes with police in Rome and Turin. Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni has announced measures, including tougher penalties for minors involved in protests. Demonstrations also occurred in other European cities, addressing issues like education, corruption, and housing. In Albania, protests turned violent, while in Spain and Portugal, demonstrators focused on pensions and housing concerns. New York's archdiocese and survivors of clergy abuse agree to $800 million legal settlement The Archdiocese of New York and attorneys for about 1,300 parishioners who say they were sexually abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims. It is the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S., following a 2024 settlement of $880 million involving the Archdiocese of Los Angeles. New York Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email Saturday to clergy confirming the settlement after attorneys for the survivors of alleged abuse announced it. Abuse survivor attorney Jeff Anderson said the settlement represents a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice. Hicks said in his email that the settlement will bring healing and reconciliation. Serbia holds a parliamentary election as strongman Vucic faces protesting students BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbians are voting in a parliamentary election seen as a showdown between strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic and a student-led movement. The election is shaping up as a referendum between Vucic's right-wing party and the Students' List. The main contenders are polling neck-and-neck, making it the most uncertain election in recent years. The European Union is closely watching the vote due to past irregularities. If his party wins, Vucic plans to return as prime minister. The Students' List, a new movement, aims to counter Vucic's rule with a non-partisan approach. items.title: Hot PPI and CPI data test Fed patience on rate hikes — NewsNovo
items.excerpt: U.S. inflationary pressures are broadening, testing the Federal Reserve's recent signals of patience on interest rates. Bureau of Labor Statistics data released this week shows price increases accelerating in both wholesale and consumer sectors, complicating the central bank's path ahead. The Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest level since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts had expected. This followed a strong reading on consumer prices released Wednesday. Additionally, September retail sales increased by 0.8%, double the 0.4% forecast, while the August figure was revised upward. Initial claims for unemployment benefits stood at 199,000, remaining near historic lows. Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin noted that the September PPI report reinforces the message from Wednesday's CPI data that inflation is moving in the wrong direction for the Fed. He added that businesses appear to be passing higher costs onto customers, as the proxy for margins rose significantly in September. Klachkin also pointed to AI-related categories as a source of upside pressure on prices. ... Fed Chair Jerome Powell faces a dilemma as he prepares for a policy meeting concluding on Oct. 28. In a speech at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand, Powell has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period. Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson have signaled in recent weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month. ... Market reactions have been mixed. Bond yields fell Thursday despite the hot PPI number, reversing a surge seen after Wednesday's CPI release. The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after Wednesday's CPI data, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead, before dropping to 4.72% Thursday morning. This move suggests a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades and semiconductor stocks decline.

items.title: California election officials frustrated, rattled by DOJ demand to sequester 'noncitizen' ballots | PBS News
items.excerpt: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Local election officials across California are confused and frustrated after receiving letters from President Donald Trump's Justice Department demanding that county registrars sequester ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections. The letters, which were sent on Friday, ask for sensitive information, including Social Security numbers, on roughly 20,000 voters. It is illegal for noncitizens to register to vote or cast a ballot. The administration has insisted that immigrants voting is a major problem nationwide, when in fact it is quite rare, as even its own investigations have shown. ... The federal government set a 48-hour deadline to provide information, and it warned that legal action could be taken against any official who knowingly counted a noncitizen's vote. ... The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between Democratic-dominated California and Trump's Department of Justice ahead of the midterms. The federal government sued on Oct. 15, roughly three weeks before elections, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens. A panel of 9th Circuit appeals court judges will hear arguments on Sunday about whether California can be compelled to comply with the federal government's demands. ... The letters on Friday came on the heels of a statewide sweep by federal authorities on Monday, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

items.title: 'This Week' Transcript 10-25-26: Rep. Ashley Hinson, Josh Turek & Gov. Wes Moore - ABC News
items.excerpt: Nine days to go and nearly every sign points in the same direction. Poll after poll shows the president’s approval rating at the lowest of his presidency. Four polls just this week show a record low for Trump. And the non-partisan Cook Political Report keeps moving races towards Democrats, even in deep red South Carolina and Mississippi. But not a single vote has been counted. And we’ve all seen election surprises. We’ve all seen polls that are wildly wrong as we do what we do, reporting on the races, talking to the experts, talking to the candidates, talking to the voters. It’s worth keeping in mind that none of us really knows how this is going to turn out. What we do know is that interest is enormous. Early voting is underway in 47 states. About 26 million Americans have already cast ballots. In Georgia, more than a million people voted in the first week alone. The first day breaking a midterm record. In Iowa, Texas, Kansas, we’ve seen signs Democratic enthusiasm and voting is up. Those are states with Republican Senate seats that Democrats hope to flip. And nine days out, the president is already laying the groundwork to challenge the results. items.title: You Can See Everything Box Office Huge Second Weekend, Clayface Leads
items.excerpt: Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-book adaptation at the domestic box office. ... Although Warner Bros. and DC’s R-rated “ Clayface” was comfortably at No. 1 with $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, A24’s buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc “ You Can See Everything” was surprisingly close after defying box office expectations again. The stranger-than-fiction film collected a spectacular $19.5 million while expanding to 2,655 venues in its sophomore outing. Ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” are 28% above its launch of $15.6 million from 855 theaters, which marked the best start for a nonmusical documentary in 20 years. So far, the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed movie has earned a huge $45.1 million domestically to date. After capturing the zeitgeist and selling out screenings across the country, awards sages are predicting it could become the first documentary to ever score a best picture nomination at the Oscars. ... “Clayface” arrived on the lower end of the studio’s expectations of $25 million to $35 million. The antihero adaptation earned another $19 million overseas from 76 markets for a global tally of $43 million. Along with a positive reception, the film seems well-positioned theatrically because it cost just $44 million to produce. That’s a way smaller budget compared to DC’s other recent tentpoles, including this July’s “Supergirl” and 2025’s “Superman.” Although “Superman” was a decent hit with $618 million against a $225 million budget, “Supergirl” was a setback for the newly relaunched comic book studio after bombing with $126 million against a $170 million budget. Meanwhile, DC has found success on streaming with its “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns” shows for HBO Max. DC wanted to keep costs low on “Clayface” because it’s a body-horror thriller that’s much darker than those family-friendly adventures. Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Audiences enjoyed the film, which holds an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls.

items.title: Harry Styles' 'Coming Up Roses' Video Quietly Announced at MSG Concert
items.excerpt: There’s a new Harry Styles music video coming up on Monday (Oct. 26) — for a song many fans have been raving about since they first heard it. Styles is releasing a “Coming Up Roses” video. The news comes straight from the star’s lips, live on stage at the famous Madison Square Garden, via an awfully casual and quiet announcement during night 27 of his 30-night concert residency Saturday night (Oct. 24). Fan footage captured the moment on video, though one might need to rewatch the clip with the volume turned up high to make sure they’ve heard what they think they heard. ... “‘Coming Up Roses’ video on Monday,” Styles said nonchalantly while seated at his piano in New York City on Saturday. The under-his-breath comment made the rounds online post-show, and by Sunday, the Spotify Canvas video clip for “Roses” was updated with a short clip of two sets of feet looking hesitantly ready to dance. ... A “Coming Up Roses” video would be the fourth one to come from the Billboard 200 No. 1 album Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally, following Styles’ visuals for Hot 100 No. 1 “Aperture,” “American Girls” and “Dance No More.” ... A beloved, poignant piano-with-strings-section ballad with regular placement on Styles’ tour setlist, “Coming Up Roses” was an immediate favorite for many fans upon first listen of Kiss All the Time in March. Styles’ historic run at MSG wraps on Halloween; nights 29 and 30, on Oct. 30-31, are dubbed the “Harryween” shows. Last weekend Billboard confirmed that there’s a documentary in the works on the experience, directed by John Wilson (How to With John Wilson, The History of Concrete) and produced by Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures and Styles. ... Future Together, Together tour dates bring Styles to Melbourne, Australia, in November-December, and then back to the U.S. thanks to a tour extension into 2027, when Styles will take the show to Phoenix, Dallas, Los Angeles, Toronto, Atlanta and Chicago in the spring, and then over to Europe in the summer.
